topics.title: Primary, secondary and tertiary sectors and GDP

learn.hook: Your morning cup of chai passes through all three sectors of the economy before it reaches your hands!
points: Primary sector: producing goods by directly using natural resources — agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry and mining. It is also called the agriculture and related sector.
Secondary sector: changing natural products into other forms through manufacturing — sugar from sugarcane, cloth from cotton, bricks from clay. It is also called the industrial sector.

Tertiary sector: activities that support the other two and produce services rather than goods — transport, storage, communication, banking and trade, plus services of teachers, doctors, lawyers and IT workers. It is also called the service sector.
The sectors depend on each other: a farmer needs transport and a market, and a textile mill needs cotton from farmers.

Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. Only final goods are counted, because the value of intermediate goods (like cotton used to make cloth) is already included in the final good's value — counting both would be double counting.

example.q: Think it through: A farmer sells sugarcane worth ₹40 to a mill. The mill makes sugar and sells it for ₹70 to a sweet shop. The sweet shop uses it to make jalebis and sells them to customers for ₹200. How much is added to GDP?
steps: Sugarcane and sugar are intermediate goods here — they are used up in making something else.
The jalebis sold to customers are the final good, worth ₹200.
The ₹200 price already includes the value of the sugar and sugarcane used.
Adding 40 + 70 + 200 = ₹310 would count the sugarcane and sugar more than once.
example.answer: ₹200 — only the value of the final good is counted.

learn.reallife: The tea leaves are plucked in Assam's gardens (primary), processed and packed in a factory (secondary), and carried by trucks and sold at your local kirana shop (tertiary).

quiz.q: Fishing belongs to which sector of the economy?
quiz.explain: Fishing directly uses a natural resource, so it is a primary sector activity.
steps: Asked: the sector of fishing.
Rule: the primary sector produces goods by directly using natural resources.
Fishing takes fish directly from rivers and seas, a natural resource.
So it is primary. 'Organised' describes job conditions, not the type of activity.
Answer: Primary sector
quiz.mistake: Confuses the type of activity with the conditions of employment

quiz.q: Making sugar from sugarcane is an activity of which sector?
quiz.explain: Sugarcane, a natural product, is changed into sugar through manufacturing — a secondary sector activity.
steps: Asked: the sector of making sugar from sugarcane.
Rule: the secondary sector changes natural products into other forms by manufacturing.
Sugarcane (a natural product) is turned into sugar in a mill.
So it is secondary. Growing the sugarcane would be primary.
Answer: Secondary sector
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything related to crops belongs to the primary sector

quiz.q: Why is the tertiary sector also called the service sector?
options: Because it manufactures goods in factories
Because it produces services rather than goods
Because only the government runs it
Because it uses natural resources directly
quiz.explain: Transport, banking, teaching and trade do not produce goods themselves; they provide services.
steps: Asked: why the tertiary sector is called the service sector.
Transport, banking, trade and teaching do not make goods themselves.
They produce services that support the other sectors and people.
So it is called the service sector.
Answer: Because it produces services rather than goods
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the tertiary sector with manufacturing

quiz.q: Which is the correct meaning of GDP?
options: The total income earned by Indians living abroad
The value of all intermediate goods produced in a year
The total amount of money printed in a year
The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year
quiz.explain: GDP measures the value of final goods and services produced within the country in one year.
steps: Asked: the meaning of GDP.
Rule: GDP = value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a particular year.
Intermediate goods are not counted separately, and GDP is not money printed or income from abroad.
Answer: The value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year
quiz.mistake: Includes intermediate goods or confuses GDP with money supply

quiz.q: A farmer sells cotton for ₹50 to a mill, the mill sells yarn for ₹80 to a weaver, and the weaver sells cloth to customers for ₹150. What value is added to GDP?
quiz.explain: Only the final good, the cloth worth ₹150, is counted. Its price already includes the cotton and yarn.
steps: Cotton and yarn are intermediate goods
Cloth sold to customers is the final good
Value counted = ₹150
quiz.mistake: Adds the values at every stage, which is double counting

quiz.q: Which of these is an intermediate good?
options: A packet of biscuits bought by a family
A bicycle bought by a student
Flour bought by a biscuit factory to make biscuits
quiz.explain: The flour is used up in making biscuits, so it is an intermediate good. The others are final goods or services used by consumers.
steps: Asked: which item is an intermediate good.
Rule: a good used up in making another good is intermediate.
Flour bought by a biscuit factory is used up to make biscuits.
Biscuits, a bicycle or a haircut bought by consumers are final goods or services.
Answer: Flour bought by a biscuit factory to make biscuits
quiz.mistake: Thinks a good's type, not its use, decides whether it is intermediate

quiz.q: Why are only final goods counted in GDP?
options: Because the value of intermediate goods is already included in the final value, so counting them would be double counting
Because intermediate goods have no value
Because the government does not allow it
quiz.explain: The price of the final good already covers the intermediate goods used to make it.
steps: Asked: why only final goods are counted in GDP.
The price of a final good already includes the intermediate goods used to make it.
Counting both would count the same value twice: double counting.
Intermediate goods do have value; it is simply already included.
Answer: Because the value of intermediate goods is already included in the final value, so counting them would be double counting
quiz.mistake: Thinks intermediate goods are worthless instead of already included

quiz.q: If all truck drivers go on strike, farmers cannot send vegetables to cities. What does this show?
options: The primary sector does not need any other sector
Farming belongs to the secondary sector
The three sectors depend on each other
quiz.explain: Farmers (primary) need transport (tertiary) to reach markets, so the sectors are interdependent.
steps: Asked: what the truck strike shows.
Farmers (primary) need transport (tertiary) to send vegetables to markets.
When transport stops, the primary sector is hurt too.
So the three sectors depend on each other.
quiz.mistake: Treats each sector as working in isolation

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his head: 'A farmer, a factory and a bank — how are they different? And what is this GDP thing?'
teach.praise: Yay! Primary uses nature, secondary manufactures, tertiary gives services — and GDP counts only final goods and services. Super clear!
teach.nudge: Which sector uses natural resources and which one gives services? And which goods does GDP count?

revise.summary: The economy has three sectors: primary (using natural resources), secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services). They depend on each other. GDP is the value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a year.
focus: Classify an activity as primary, secondary or tertiary
Tell final goods from intermediate goods
Work out the value added to GDP without double counting
Explain how the sectors depend on each other
remember: Primary: agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining (agriculture and related sector)
Secondary: manufacturing, such as sugar from sugarcane (industrial sector)
Tertiary: transport, storage, communication, banking, trade, services (service sector)
GDP: value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year
traps: Don't add the value at every stage; count only the final good
Making sugar from sugarcane is secondary, not primary
Don't confuse the type of activity with organised or public sector

learn.hook: Five people working on a field that needs only three — everyone looks busy, but is everyone really needed?
points: In the early stages of development, the primary sector was the most important. As farming improved and produced more food, people moved to manufacturing and the secondary sector became most important. In developed countries today, the tertiary sector is the most important.
In India, production has grown in all three sectors, but most in the tertiary sector, which has become the largest producing sector, replacing the primary sector.

Reasons for tertiary growth: basic services like hospitals, schools, post offices, police, courts and banks are needed; growing farms and factories need more transport, trade and storage; rising incomes create demand for services like eating out, tourism and private schools; new IT-based services have grown fast. But many tertiary workers, like small shopkeepers and repair workers, still earn very little.

Jobs did not shift the same way: the primary sector is still the largest employer in India, even though its share in GDP is much smaller. The secondary and tertiary sectors have not created enough jobs.

Disguised unemployment (underemployment): more people work than are needed, so if some leave, output does not fall. It is common in farming and also among urban casual workers who have work only part of the time.

More jobs can come from irrigation, rural roads, storage and cheap credit, agro-processing units, tourism, health and education. The textbook also describes MGNREGA 2005, a law that guaranteed 100 days of work in a year to rural people who needed and could do work, with an unemployment allowance if work was not given. Update: in December 2025 a new law, the Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-G RAM G), was passed to replace MGNREGA from 1 July 2026; it guarantees 125 days of wage work in a year. For your exam, learn MGNREGA as the textbook describes it.

example.q: Think it through: Meena's family of 5 works on a small 2-hectare farm. The farm needs only 3 workers. Two family members find jobs in a nearby town and production stays the same. What does this show?
steps: Before, 5 people worked but only 3 were really needed.
When 2 left, output did not fall, so their labour was adding nothing extra.
This is disguised unemployment: people appear employed but are not fully productive.
The 2 members can now add to the family income from the town, so the family is better off.
example.answer: 2 members were disguisedly unemployed; moving them to other work raises total income.

learn.reallife: On a city street, many painters and plumbers wait at a chowk every morning for daily work; many get work only on some days — another form of underemployment.

games.title: Sectors and jobs: true or false?
items: In India, the tertiary sector has become the largest producing sector.
Its share of production grew the most and it replaced the primary sector.

quiz.q: Which sector has become the largest producing sector in India?
quiz.explain: Production grew fastest in the tertiary sector, which replaced the primary sector as the largest producer.
steps: Asked: India's largest producing sector.
Production grew in all three sectors, but most in the tertiary sector.
The tertiary sector replaced the primary sector as the largest producer.
Don't confuse this with the largest employer, which is still primary.
Answer: Tertiary sector
quiz.mistake: Confuses the largest producer with the largest employer

quiz.q: Which sector still employs the largest number of workers in India?
quiz.explain: Most workers are still in the primary sector, mainly agriculture, although its share in GDP is much smaller.
steps: Asked: the sector employing the most workers in India.
Jobs did not shift the way production did.
The primary sector is still the largest employer, though its share in GDP is much smaller.
So the answer is the primary sector.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the sector producing most also employs most

quiz.q: Kamla's family of 5 works on a plot that needs only 3 workers. How many family members are disguisedly unemployed?
quiz.explain: Only 3 are needed, so 5 − 3 = 2 members are not really adding to output.
steps: Workers present = 5
Workers needed = 3
Extra workers = 5 − 3 = 2
quiz.mistake: Gives the number needed instead of the extra workers

quiz.q: Which is a reason for the growth of the tertiary sector in India?
options: Rising incomes increase demand for services like restaurants, tourism and private schools
Farming has completely stopped in India
quiz.explain: As incomes rise, people spend more on services, which helps the tertiary sector grow.
steps: Asked: a real reason for tertiary growth.
Lesson: rising incomes raise demand for services like eating out, tourism and private schools.
The other options are false claims: farming has not stopped and factories still need transport.
Answer: Rising incomes increase demand for services like restaurants, tourism and private schools
quiz.mistake: Picks an exaggerated claim instead of a real cause

quiz.q: What is disguised unemployment?
options: When workers are on a paid holiday
When people have no work at all and say so openly
When workers move abroad for jobs
When more people work than needed, so some are not really productive
quiz.explain: In disguised unemployment, everyone seems to be working, but removing some workers would not reduce output.
steps: Asked: the meaning of disguised unemployment.
More people work than are needed, so if some leave, output does not fall.
Everyone seems employed, but some are not really productive.
Having no work at all and saying so is open unemployment, not disguised.
Answer: When more people work than needed, so some are not really productive
quiz.mistake: Confuses hidden underemployment with open unemployment

quiz.q: Historically, as countries developed, which sector became the most important after the primary sector?
quiz.explain: Better farming freed people to work in manufacturing, so the secondary sector became most important next; the tertiary sector rose later.
steps: Asked: the next most important sector after the primary sector.
As farming improved and produced more food, people moved to manufacturing.
So the secondary sector became most important next; the tertiary sector rose later.
quiz.mistake: Skips the industrial stage and jumps to services

quiz.q: As described in the textbook, MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed rural people who needed work how many days of employment in a year?
quiz.explain: The textbook explains that MGNREGA 2005 guaranteed 100 days of employment in a year, and an unemployment allowance if work was not provided. (Update: from 1 July 2026 MGNREGA is replaced by the VB-G RAM G Act, 2025, which guarantees 125 days.)
steps: Asked: the days of work under MGNREGA 2005, as the textbook says.
The textbook says it guaranteed 100 days of work a year to rural people who needed work.
So the answer is 100 days. (Update: VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 replaces it from 1 July 2026 with 125 days.)
quiz.mistake: Guesses a number instead of recalling the 100-day guarantee

quiz.q: Which step would best create more jobs in a village where farmers grow only one crop a year?
options: Banning farmers from selling in towns
Building wells or canals for irrigation
quiz.explain: Irrigation lets farmers grow a second crop, which needs more workers and creates more jobs.
steps: Asked: the step that best creates more village jobs.
With only one crop a year, there is farm work for only part of the year.
Wells or canals for irrigation let farmers grow a second crop, which needs more workers.
Closing schools or cutting roads would reduce work, not add it.
Answer: Building wells or canals for irrigation
quiz.mistake: Does not link irrigation to more farm work

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'If services now make the most money in India, then most people must work in services. Right? And what is disguised unemployment?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! Services produce the most, but farming still employs the most — and many farm workers are disguisedly unemployed. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: Which sector produces most and which employs most? And what happens to output when the extra workers leave?

revise.summary: In India the tertiary sector has become the largest producer, but the primary sector is still the largest employer. Many farm workers are disguisedly unemployed, and schemes like MGNREGA aim to create more jobs.

remember: Tertiary sector: largest producing sector in India; primary sector: largest employer
Disguised unemployment: more people work than needed, so output does not fall if some leave
MGNREGA 2005 (textbook): 100 days of work a year, with unemployment allowance if work is not given
Update: VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 replaces MGNREGA from 1 July 2026 and guarantees 125 days

Disguised unemployment is not open unemployment; the workers seem to be working
Historically the secondary sector came before the tertiary sector became most important

learn.hook: Two people both work 8 hours a day — one gets paid leave and a pension, the other can lose the job tomorrow. What's the difference?
points: Organised sector: enterprises or places of work with regular terms of employment. They are registered by the government and must follow laws such as the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act. (Update: since 21 November 2025 the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and many other central labour laws have been combined into four new Labour Codes; the idea of the organised sector stays the same.)

Organised-sector workers get job security, fixed working hours, extra pay for overtime, paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits and often a pension after retirement.

Unorganised sector: small, scattered units largely outside government control. Rules exist but are often not followed. Jobs are low-paid and irregular, with no overtime pay, paid leave or sick leave, and workers can be removed without reason.

Many people work in the unorganised sector: in villages — landless labourers, small and marginal farmers, sharecroppers and artisans; in towns — casual construction workers, street vendors, head-load workers, garment workers in small units and rag pickers.
Unorganised workers need protection: the government can fix minimum wages and working hours, and help small units with cheap loans, raw materials and marketing.

example.q: Think it through: Sunil works in a registered car-parts factory with a written contract, paid leave and provident fund. His cousin Raju works at a small roadside workshop, is paid in cash daily and gets nothing when he falls ill. Which sector does each belong to?
steps: Sunil's job has regular terms, is registered and gives benefits like paid leave and provident fund.
These are features of the organised sector.
Raju's job is irregular, has no leave or security and follows no formal rules.
These are features of the unorganised sector.
example.answer: Sunil — organised sector; Raju — unorganised sector.

learn.reallife: The person who sells bhutta near your school, the helper at a small dhaba and the daily-wage worker building a house are mostly in the unorganised sector; a bank clerk or a railway engineer is in the organised sector.

games.title: Organised or unorganised?
items: Bank clerk with salary slip and provident fund
Worker in a registered factory who gets paid leave
Government school teacher with a pension
Railway engineer with fixed working hours
Street vendor selling bhutta
Daily-wage construction labourer

games.title: Organised vs unorganised: true or false?
items: Organised-sector enterprises are registered by the government.
Registration means they must follow government rules and laws.
Unorganised-sector workers usually get paid sick leave.
Unorganised jobs usually have no paid leave or sick leave.
Provident fund and gratuity are benefits of organised-sector jobs.
These are given under the laws that organised enterprises follow.
In the unorganised sector, workers can be asked to leave without any reason.
There is little job security in the unorganised sector.
A head-load worker in a mandi works in the organised sector.
Such work is irregular, casual and has no benefits, so it is unorganised.
Fixing minimum wages can help protect unorganised workers.
It guarantees a basic wage, reducing exploitation.

quiz.q: Which of these is a feature of the organised sector?
options: Workers can be removed without reason
Wages paid only when there is work
quiz.explain: Organised-sector workers get benefits such as paid leave, provident fund and job security.
steps: Asked: a feature of the organised sector.
Organised-sector workers get job security, paid leave, provident fund and overtime pay.
No fixed hours, removal without reason and pay only when there is work describe the unorganised sector.
So 'paid leave and provident fund' is correct.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the features of the two sectors

quiz.q: Organised-sector enterprises are those that are:
options: Registered by the government and follow its rules and regulations
quiz.explain: The key feature is registration and following laws; a privately owned firm can also be in the organised sector.
steps: Asked: what makes an enterprise part of the organised sector.
Rule: it is registered by the government and must follow its rules and laws.
It need not be government-owned or very large; a private firm can be organised.
Answer: Registered by the government and follow its rules and regulations
quiz.mistake: Confuses organised (employment conditions) with public (ownership)

quiz.q: A woman sells vegetables from a handcart on the street. She has no fixed income and no leave. Which sector is she in?
quiz.explain: Her work is irregular, unregistered and without benefits, so it is in the unorganised sector.
steps: Asked: the sector of a street vegetable seller.
Her work is irregular, unregistered and has no fixed income or leave.
These are features of the unorganised sector.
Selling is a tertiary activity, but the question is about job conditions.
Answer: Unorganised sector
quiz.mistake: Does not link irregular work without benefits to the unorganised sector

quiz.q: Rakesh works overtime in a registered factory. What is he entitled to under organised-sector rules?
quiz.explain: In the organised sector, employers must pay extra for overtime work.
steps: Asked: what Rakesh gets for overtime in a registered factory.
Organised-sector rules give workers extra pay for overtime.
So he is entitled to extra payment for the overtime.
quiz.mistake: Assumes extra hours are always unpaid

quiz.q: Why do unorganised-sector workers need protection?
options: Because they get very high salaries
Because their jobs are low-paid, irregular and without security
Because they work only for the government
quiz.explain: Unorganised workers face low pay, irregular work and no job security, so they need support and protection.
steps: Asked: why unorganised workers need protection.
Their jobs are low-paid and irregular, with no paid leave, sick leave or security.
They can be removed without reason.
So they need protection; they do not have high salaries or pensions.
Answer: Because their jobs are low-paid, irregular and without security
quiz.mistake: Thinks unorganised workers already have enough benefits

quiz.q: The textbook lists laws about workers that organised-sector enterprises must follow. Which of these is one of them?
quiz.explain: The Minimum Wages Act, like the Factories Act and the Payment of Gratuity Act, sets rules about workers' pay and conditions. The other laws deal with information, wildlife and elections. (Since November 2025 these labour laws have been combined into four Labour Codes.)
steps: Asked: a law about workers that organised firms must follow.
The textbook lists the Factories Act, Minimum Wages Act, Payment of Gratuity Act and Shops and Establishments Act.
The Minimum Wages Act is on this list.
RTI, wildlife and election laws are not about employment.
Answer: Minimum Wages Act
quiz.mistake: Picks a real law that is not about employment conditions

quiz.q: Which group of workers is mostly found in the unorganised sector in rural areas?
quiz.explain: Landless labourers, small farmers, sharecroppers and artisans usually have irregular work and no benefits.
steps: Asked: rural workers mostly in the unorganised sector.
In villages, landless labourers, small farmers, sharecroppers and artisans have irregular work and no benefits.
Bank managers, government doctors and clerks have regular jobs in the organised sector.
Answer: Landless labourers, sharecroppers and artisans
quiz.mistake: Thinks all rural work is organised

quiz.q: Which government step would most directly help small units in the unorganised sector?
options: Increasing the working hours without extra pay
Stopping all loans to small producers
Providing cheap loans, raw materials and help in marketing
quiz.explain: Cheap credit, raw materials and marketing help let small units earn more and survive.
steps: Asked: the step that most directly helps small unorganised units.
The government can help small units with cheap loans, raw materials and marketing.
Removing minimum wages, unpaid extra hours or stopping loans would make things worse.
Answer: Providing cheap loans, raw materials and help in marketing
quiz.mistake: Chooses a step that would make conditions worse

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Both my uncles work all day. One gets paid holidays and one doesn't. Why? Explain organised and unorganised sectors!'
teach.praise: Chirp! Organised jobs are registered and follow rules with benefits; unorganised jobs are irregular with no security. You nailed it!
teach.nudge: Which sector follows government rules? What benefits do workers there get that others don't?

revise.summary: The organised sector has registered units with regular jobs and benefits like paid leave, provident fund and overtime pay. The unorganised sector has small, scattered units with low-paid, irregular jobs and no security, so its workers need protection.
focus: Features of organised vs unorganised sector jobs
Classify a given worker into the right sector
Who works in the unorganised sector in villages and towns
How the government can protect unorganised workers
remember: Organised: registered by government, follows laws like the Factories Act and Minimum Wages Act
Organised benefits: job security, fixed hours, overtime pay, paid leave, provident fund, gratuity, medical benefits
Unorganised: low-paid, irregular, no paid leave, workers can be removed without reason
Update: since 21 November 2025 many central labour laws are combined into four Labour Codes
traps: Organised does not mean government-owned; a private firm can be organised
Don't mix up the features of the two sectors
A street vendor is in the unorganised sector even though selling is a tertiary activity

learn.hook: The train you ride and the biscuit you munch on it are made by two very different kinds of owners!
points: Sectors can also be classified by who owns the assets. In the public sector, the government owns most of the assets and provides the services, like the Indian Railways and post offices.
In the private sector, assets are owned and services delivered by private individuals or companies.
The private sector's main motive is to earn profits. The public sector's aim is not just profit but public welfare; the government raises money through taxes to pay for its services.

Some things need huge spending that the private sector will not provide at a reasonable cost: roads, bridges, railways, harbours, generating electricity and irrigation through dams. It is also hard to collect money from thousands of users, so the government provides these.

The government also supports private activity — for example, it sells electricity at low rates to industries, and buys wheat and rice from farmers at a fair price, stores them and sells them at lower prices through ration shops. It also has a duty to provide health and education facilities for all.

example.q: Think it through: Why would a private company not want to build a long bridge connecting a few villages across a river?
steps: Building a bridge costs a huge amount of money.
Collecting a fee from every villager who walks or cycles across would be very hard.
The private company could not earn enough profit, so it would not invest.
The government, which aims at public welfare and collects taxes, can build it for everyone.
example.answer: Because it is too costly and unprofitable for a private company; the government builds it for public welfare.

learn.reallife: When your family buys rice and wheat at a lower price from the local ration shop, you see the government supporting both farmers and consumers.

quiz.q: On what basis are sectors classified as public and private?
options: Who owns the assets and delivers the services
quiz.explain: Public and private sectors are classified by ownership.
steps: Asked: the basis of the public/private classification.
Public and private sectors differ in who owns the assets and delivers the services.
Activity type is the basis for primary/secondary/tertiary; job conditions for organised/unorganised.
So the basis is ownership.
Answer: Who owns the assets and delivers the services
quiz.mistake: Confuses ownership with activity type or employment conditions

quiz.q: Indian Railways belongs to which sector?
quiz.explain: The government owns and runs the Indian Railways, so it is in the public sector.
steps: Asked: the sector of Indian Railways.
The government owns and runs Indian Railways.
When the government owns most assets and provides the service, it is the public sector.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a large service provider must be private

quiz.q: What is the main motive of the private sector?
quiz.explain: Private owners invest to earn profits.
steps: Asked: the main motive of the private sector.
Private individuals or companies invest to earn profits.
Public welfare is the public sector's aim, and collecting taxes is the government's job.
So the answer is earning profit.
quiz.mistake: Assigns the public sector's aim to the private sector

quiz.q: How does the government mainly raise money for public sector services?
options: By selling shares on the stock market every day
quiz.explain: The government collects taxes from people and businesses to pay for public services.
steps: Asked: how the government mainly funds public services.
The government raises money through taxes on people and businesses.
It uses this money to pay for public services.
Answer: Through taxes
quiz.mistake: Does not know that taxes fund public services

quiz.q: Why does the government usually build roads, bridges and dams?
options: Because private companies are not allowed to build anything
Because they need huge spending and it is hard to collect money from all users, so private firms won't provide them at a reasonable cost
Because they earn very high profits
Because only the government knows engineering
quiz.explain: These projects cost a lot and are hard to charge every user for, so the government provides them for public welfare.
steps: Asked: why the government builds roads, bridges and dams.
They need huge spending, and it is hard to collect money from thousands of users.
So private firms will not provide them at a reasonable cost.
The government provides them for public welfare; they are not highly profitable.
Answer: Because they need huge spending and it is hard to collect money from all users, so private firms won't provide them at a reasonable cost
quiz.mistake: Thinks such projects are left to the government because they are highly profitable

quiz.q: The government buys wheat from farmers at a fair price and sells it at a lower price through ration shops. Whom does this help?
quiz.explain: Farmers get a fair price and poor consumers get cheaper grain; the government bears part of the cost.
steps: Asked: whom the wheat scheme helps.
The government buys wheat from farmers at a fair price, which helps farmers.
It sells the wheat at lower prices through ration shops, which helps poor consumers.
So it helps both farmers and poor consumers.
quiz.mistake: Misses that the scheme supports both sides

quiz.q: A chain of hospitals is owned by a group of private shareholders. Which sector does it belong to?
quiz.explain: Ownership by private shareholders puts it in the private sector; a hospital's activity is in the tertiary sector.
steps: Asked: the sector of a hospital chain owned by private shareholders.
Ownership decides public vs private.
Private shareholders own it, so it is in the private sector.
Its activity (health care) is tertiary, not primary or secondary.
Answer: Private sector
quiz.mistake: Thinks all hospitals belong to the public sector

quiz.q: Dividing the economy into organised and unorganised sectors is based on:
quiz.explain: Organised and unorganised sectors differ in terms of employment — rules, security and benefits.
steps: Asked: the basis of the organised/unorganised division.
Organised and unorganised sectors differ in rules, job security and benefits.
These are conditions of employment.
Ownership is the basis for public/private; activity for primary/secondary/tertiary.
Answer: Conditions of employment
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the three bases of classification

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Who owns the train I ride and the biscuit factory? Why doesn't one company just build all the roads?'
teach.praise: Hooray! The public sector is owned by the government for public welfare; the private sector is owned by people or companies for profit. Perfect!
teach.nudge: Who owns each sector, and what is each one's main aim — profit or welfare?

revise.summary: By ownership, the economy has a public sector (government owns assets, aims at public welfare, funded by taxes) and a private sector (private owners, aims at profit). The government provides costly facilities like roads, dams and railways, and supports farmers and consumers.
focus: Classify an enterprise as public or private by ownership
Motive of each sector and how the government funds services
Why the government provides roads, bridges, railways, dams and electricity
The three bases of classifying sectors
remember: Public sector: government owns most assets, e.g. Indian Railways, post offices
Private sector: owned by private individuals or companies; main motive is profit
Government raises money through taxes to pay for public services
traps: Don't mix up the three bases of classification
Not all hospitals are public; a privately owned hospital is in the private sector
The government builds roads and dams because they are costly and hard to charge for, not because they are profitable
